title: The Recruit
full_review:
A rookie's training at the Central Intelligence Agency proves madly eventful in the sleek romantic thriller, "The Recruit" (Touchstone). The CIA actually cooperated and the movie romanticizes the recruitment and training process as filled with one dangerous thrill after another.

Director Roger Donaldson is back in the Washington-suspense territory he captured so effectively in 1987's "No Way Out." This time the milieu is the inner workings of the CIA, but it opens in Boston where veteran operative Walter Burke (Al Pacino) entices MIT grad and computer whiz James Clayton (Colin Farrell) to join the agency by implying the young man's dad was a crack CIA agent. James is hooked, especially as his father went missing under murky circumstances when he was 12, and he hopes Burke can fill in the blanks.

Training classes at the facility known as "The Farm" consist of gruesome mental, physical and psychological tests. "Trust no one" and "nothing is at it seems," Burke stresses, but James' attention also focuses on fellow recruit Layla (Bridget Moynahan). When he fails a test and is cut from the program, Burke reveals Layla is a mole in their midst -- and wants James to get the goods on her. By pretending he now has a regular staff job with the agency, he can continue to see Layla and discover how she is ferreting out sensitive information and to whom she is giving it.

Reluctantly, he accepts the assignment -- and, far from reluctantly, takes Layla to bed. James wants to prove she is not a traitor, but he soon finds out how true it is that nothing is what it appears to be.

Donaldson maintains suspense and a brisk pace in equal parts, which makes for an engrossing thriller. But it doesn't pack the surprise that "No Way Out" offered; there aren't many key characters, making it fairly easy to divine who's dirty on The Farm. The trust-no-one theme is overplayed where subtlety would have improved the whodunit aspect of the tale. Nonetheless, the serpentine twists are always involving, as layer after layer of deceit is peeled away.

Farrell and Pacino play well off one another. Pacino gives a solid performance, though not at the level of last year's "Insomnia." Farrell, showing a fluctuating one-to-three-day growth of beard in the same scenes, seems to be following Brad Pitt's trajectory of gradually building up to lead-actor status.

The action-chase sequences are efficiently filmed, and there is comparatively little violence for a film in this genre. Primarily shot in Toronto, there are enough background shots of Washington landmarks to give it an air of authenticity. The espionage game is rife with moral ambiguities but this movie favors black-and-white characters with no shades of gray lurking in the shadows.

"The Recruit" is likely to sign up its target young-male audience -- and do double duty in recruiting candidates for the CIA.

Due to brief violence and torture, an implied affair, occasional profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
